A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Question a, other: The clue ('what happens to rock that sticks, then slips') nearly restates the right option, 'Stuck plates build up stress, then slip', so students can match words without knowing the idea.
- Question b, wording: The right option is the only hedged one ('A few ... can'). The distractors use 'only' and 'must', so a test-wise student can pick the answer without understanding the idea.

rejected.title: Earthquakes and volcanoes
card: Most earthquakes and volcanoes happen along plate boundaries. Few happen in the middle of a plate.
Earthquakes
Plates grind past each other or push together and get stuck. Stress builds up. When the rock suddenly slips, the energy is released as shaking.
Volcanoes
Where one plate sinks under another, or where plates pull apart, rock can melt. The melted rock (magma) rises and erupts at the surface.
The Pacific Ring of Fire is a long belt of boundaries around the Pacific Ocean. It has many of the world's earthquakes and volcanoes.
rejected.remember: Plate boundaries are where the stress builds and the rock melts, so most quakes and volcanoes are there.

a.q: Why do most earthquakes happen along plate boundaries?
opts: Stuck plates build up stress, then slip and release it
Plate edges melt, and the liquid rock shakes the ground
The core is closest to the surface at plate boundaries
Plates stop moving at their edges, so the ground is weak
a.why: Where plates grind or push together, they can stick and build up stress. When the rock slips, the energy is released as shaking. Melting is linked to volcanoes, not to the shaking of an earthquake.
a.clue: Think about what happens to rock that sticks, then slips.

b.q: A volcano erupts on an island in the middle of the Pacific plate, far from any plate boundary. What does this show?
opts: A few volcanoes can form away from plate boundaries
The island must sit on a hidden plate boundary
The Ring of Fire now reaches the middle of the Pacific
Volcanoes form only where two plates pull apart
b.why: The island is far from any boundary, yet a volcano erupts there, so a few volcanoes form away from boundaries. This fits the idea that most volcanoes, not all, are on boundaries. Saying the island must be on a hidden boundary is tempting, but the question tells you it is far from any boundary.
b.clue: Take the island's position as a fact, then test each option.

Volcanoes

version.remember: Most quakes and volcanoes are at plate boundaries: quakes where plates stick and slip, volcanoes where rock can melt.

a.q: Earthquakes are common along plate boundaries. What causes the shaking there?
opts: Stress builds in stuck rock until it suddenly slips
Gaps between plates let the crust sink and drop
The core comes closest to the surface at boundaries
Plates stop moving at their edges, which weakens rock
a.why: Where plates grind past or push into each other, the rock can stick while stress builds up. When it suddenly slips, the energy is released as shaking. Plates do not stop at their edges: the push from the moving plates is what builds the stress.
a.clue: Think about where the energy for the shaking comes from.

b.q: Hawaii's volcanoes erupt in the middle of the Pacific plate, far from any plate boundary. How does this fit the idea about where volcanoes form?
opts: Most volcanoes are at boundaries, but a few are not
Most volcanoes are at boundaries, so Hawaii is on one
Most volcanoes are mid-plate, as Hawaii's are
Most volcanoes form where plates pull apart, as here
b.why: The card says most volcanoes are at plate boundaries and few are in the middle of a plate, so Hawaii is one of the few. Saying Hawaii is on a boundary is tempting, but the question says it is far from any boundary. Mid-plate volcanoes are uncommon, which is why Hawaii stands out.
b.clue: Trust what the question says about where Hawaii is.
